name: bluewater-28-register
lines: In eighteen eighty four, a man bought a company that made a machine nobody wanted.
Shop owners did not want it. Their staff hated it.
Years later, it sat on shop counters around the world.
His name was John Patterson. And to sell that machine, he invented most of what we now call sales.
Here is his story. And four moves you can use.
Dayton, Ohio. A saloon owner named James Ritty has a problem. Money keeps going missing from the till.
So he builds a machine. Every sale rings a bell. And every sale is counted.
He calls it a cash register. Almost nobody buys one.
But one customer is a coal merchant called John Patterson.
His shop has been losing money. And he cannot see where.
He puts in the registers. And the books finally add up.
So he does something bold. He buys the company that makes them.
And he finds out why it was for sale.
Shopkeepers say they trust their staff. And the staff take the machine as an insult.
His first big mailing goes to five thousand shops. It gets not one reply.
He later said why. The letter had no picture of the machine.
Move one. Show the thing. Do not just describe it.
Most of his salesmen sell almost nothing. One sells a lot. His brother in law, Joseph Crane.
Patterson asks him how he does it.
Crane does not make it up as he goes. He says the same words, in the same order, every time.
So Patterson has it written down. Word for word.
He calls it the Primer. And every salesman has to learn it by heart.
It is the first known sales script.
Move two. Find what your best person says. Then have everyone say it.
But writing it down is not enough.
In eighteen ninety three, he tests his salesmen. At the World's Fair in Chicago.
Most of them do not know the script.
So he does something new. He opens a school. For selling.
A classroom in Dayton. Salesmen in rows. Practising the talk on each other.
They learn the script. And they learn an answer for every reason a customer says no.
Move three. Train it. Do not hope for it.
Then he draws lines on a map. Every salesman gets his own territory.
And every territory gets a target. A number to hit.
Now he can see who is selling. And who is not.
Estimates at the time said the training doubled the business in its first year.
Move four. Give everyone a number.
The machine nobody wanted ended up on counters around the world.
Not because it changed. Because of how it was sold.
Before Patterson, selling was a talent. You had it, or you did not.
After him, it was a process. Something you could write down, teach, and measure.
So here are the four. One. Show it. A picture. A demo. The real thing.
Two. Write down what works. And have everyone use it.
Three. Practise the hard questions before the customer asks them.
And four. Track it. A number for every person. Every week.
Your business. Our marketing department. Bluewater Co.
